messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Vignette:
Robert, a 78-year-old North American man who was divorced and living alone, had spent most of his adult life working as a database administrator, a role that fit his preference for order, precision, and long stretches of quiet concentration. Before the illness, he had understood his life as steady and predictable. That sense of stability was shattered when he developed a life-threatening medical condition that required urgent hospital treatment. In the early hours of that event, he found himself surrounded by the smell of antiseptic, plastic tubing, and the stale hospital air in a room that seemed to narrow around him as he struggled to make sense of what was happening. The memory of that period remained with him in a way that ordinary recollections did not. When he spoke about it, he often described it as if he were back there again, not simply remembering but re-entering the scene, with the hospital room, the equipment, and the bodily panic feeling immediate and present. Even years later, he could sometimes catch the same smell in the hospital corridor or in a clinic and feel a sudden tightening in his chest, as though the danger had returned without warning.

After he recovered enough to leave the hospital, Robert found that the experience had not ended when the medical crisis ended. He became increasingly wary in ways that surprised him. At home, he was not able to settle fully, even in the familiar rooms that had once felt like a refuge. He described being on guard inside his own house, listening for changes in his breathing, scanning the dark hallway at night, and feeling that he needed to stay alert in case something went wrong with his body again. He was especially troubled by the force of the feelings that came with these moments: fear, anger, and shame would rise quickly and feel too large for the situation in front of him. He had come to believe that his body could not be trusted, that it might begin reacting as if he were still in danger even when he knew he was safe in his chair, in his kitchen, or lying in bed. This was not a vague idea for him but a lived frustration, as if his body had become an unreliable companion that might betray him without notice.

Robert’s memories of the illness were unusually vivid and real to him, more immediate than many ordinary events from his long life. He could call up the specific fluorescent light, the sound of hospital carts, and most vividly the smell that clung to the sheets and his own skin. At times, when those images surfaced, he felt pulled back into the fear of that period with such intensity that he had to stop what he was doing. He was aware that the memory did not behave like a normal recollection. Rather than sitting in the past, it arrived with a force that made him momentarily uncertain about where he was in time. That sense of the event being alive in his mind left him uneasy and watchful, as though he needed to brace for an emergency that might still be unfolding.

Over time, Robert’s understanding of the world changed. He had once trusted that life was generally safe if one behaved carefully and did the right things, but after the illness he no longer felt that way. He spoke bluntly about having lost faith in people, life, and any larger power that might be supposed to protect him. What had happened to his body had left him feeling that the world was dangerous and that security could disappear without warning. This was part of why he remained so vigilant at home and why he checked and rechecked ordinary sensations, watching for the slightest sign that something was wrong. He kept working as a database administrator for as long as he could, but his concentration was increasingly interrupted by the need to monitor his body and his surroundings. The routines of daily life, which had once anchored him, now felt fragile.

By the time he sought help, Robert was exhausted by the strain of living with constant alertness and by how often the hospital memory intruded on the present. He came because he no longer wanted to keep feeling as though danger might be sitting inside his own body or waiting in his own home. What frightened him most was the possibility that this state might never ease, and what he still hoped for was some way to feel safe again in the ordinary places of his life.
